item.title: People Who Write Interestingly
item.description:
I want to share a list of people on the internet who write interesting content on product-adjacent topics and are worth following. I often return to articles from these authors — especially when I’m looking for creative inspiration.

  • Marty Cagan — an iconic figure in the product world and author of a popular series of books: Inspired, Empowered, and Transformed. Founder of SVPG and an active blogger on product management. His ideas about product discovery and empowered teams have become industry standards.
  • Paul Graham — co-founder of Y Combinator and author of wonderful essays that remain relevant across time. He writes about startups, thinking, and decision-making — concisely, precisely, and without fluff.
  • Andrew Chen — partner at Andreessen Horowitz and author of a popular blog on growth marketing.
  • Vitalik Buterin — founder of Ethereum and a prolific blogger. He writes deep technical and philosophical essays on decentralization and the future of technology.
  • Grigory Bakunov — founder of radio-t, former Director of Technology Dissemination at Yandex. Writes about technology, management, and life in tech — sharply and without corporate-speak.
  • Oleg Yakubenkov — founder of GoPractice and author of the most popular product analytics blog in the Russian-speaking market. His simulators and articles are must-reads for anyone looking to get a handle on metrics and unit economics.
  • Artem Gorbunov & Co. — a collection of practical advice on product topics from cult-status specialists. Short and to the point — covering writing, interfaces, negotiations, and management.
  • Melissa Perri — author of Escaping the Build Trap. She writes about product as a value system, product culture, and why companies get stuck in feature factory mode.
  • Teresa Torres — author of Continuous Discovery Habits. Her blog covers discovery practices: opportunity solution trees, customer interviews, and the habits of strong product teams.
  • Wes Kao — runs an excellent applied blog on management, product thinking, and career development. Publishes regularly.
  • Ben Thompson — technology analyst and author of the Stratechery blog. He takes a deep dive into the business strategies of tech companies, platform models, and competitive market dynamics.
  • Valeria Rozova — product leader and curator of an article library on product topics written by graduates of her courses. The articles are highly practical and detailed — a great resource for developing specific product skills.

item.title: Books and Materials for Product Managers
item.description:
There’s no shortage of materials online for developing product skills and broadening your horizons. But I want to gather only the most useful, practical, and valuable ones here. This list is constantly evolving: new materials are added, outdated ones are removed. I hope you find something worth your time.

Introduction to Product Culture and the Profession

  • Essay «How to Do Great Work,» Paul Graham. An essay by the iconic Paul Graham on how to do your work well — full of advice and reflection. Recommended reading for everyone starting out in their career, not just product managers.
  • Article «Good Product Manager / Bad Product Manager,» Ben Horowitz. A short article written in 2012 that remains just as relevant today. It gives a clear sense of what qualities a good product manager should have.
  • Article «Amazon Leadership Principles,» Amazon. Amazon’s 14 leadership principles — what the company expects from its managers, and what interviewers will probe during Amazon interview loops. If they don’t resonate on first read, it’s worth coming back to them later.

Managing Yourself and Your Teams

  • «Getting Things Done,» David Allen
  • «Jedi Techniques,» Maxim Dorofeev
  • «Herding Cats,» J. Hank Rainwater
  • «Managing Humans,» Michael Lopp

Research

  • «The Mom Test,» Rob Fitzpatrick. An essential classic on preparing for user interviews. The approach has its fans and its critics alike — but everyone has read it, and no one has been left indifferent.
  • «Running Lean: Iterate from Plan A to a Plan That Works,» Ash Maurya
  • Video «How to Talk to Users,» Eric Migicovsky (Y Combinator)
  • Video «ABCDX Segmentation,» Artem Azevich (IIDF Accelerator)
  • Video «Market Sizing,» Alexander Skurikhin (IIDF Accelerator, Yandex)
  • producthunt.com

Analytics

  • «Playing with Numbers: How Analytics Helps Video Games Thrive,» Vasily Sabirov. Probably the only book on product analytics written by a Russian author. It reads less like a textbook and more like a conversation with a product analyst.
  • «Say It with Charts,» Gene Zelazny
  • GoPractice Blog. Simply an encyclopedia of product analytics and product management knowledge. The articles are exceptionally well written. Best read slowly and carefully — evening tea in hand.
  • Free course «Fundamentals of Statistics and A/B Testing» by Yandex Practicum. An excellent introductory course on statistics and A/B testing, built by a team of mathematicians at Practicum.
  • Free course «Fundamentals of Statistics» by Anatoly Karpov. The most popular statistics course in the Russian-speaking web — Anatoly breaks down both descriptive and inferential statistics in a clear, structured way. It has become a classic in the Runet.

Strategy

  • «Good Strategy Bad Strategy,» Richard Rumelt. A foundational conceptual book on strategy. It explains what good strategy looks like — and what bad strategy looks like (which is most of what passes for strategy). There’s a short summary on my blog.
  • «The Goal: A Process of Ongoing Improvement,» Eliyahu Goldratt

Delivery Management / Backlog Management

  • «Getting Real: The Smarter, Faster, Easier Way to Build a Successful Web Application,» Jason Fried + David Heinemeier Hansson + Matthew Linderman
  • Article «20 Product Prioritization Techniques: A Map and Guided Tour». A detailed breakdown of 20 techniques for prioritizing your backlog or hypotheses.
  • Article «RICE: Simple prioritization for product managers,» Intercom. The original article from Intercom, where this prioritization method was born. It also includes an XLS template you can use right out of the box.

Interviews and Hiring

  • «The Art of Recruiting: How to Evaluate a Person in One Hour,» Svetlana Ivanova
  • «Who: The A Method for Hiring,» Geoff Smart and Randy Street
  • «Cracking the PM Interview: How to Land a Product Manager Job in Technology,» Gayle Laakmann McDowell
  • «Decode and Conquer,» Lewis C. Lin. One of Lewis Lin’s books — though if you can, it’s worth reading his others as well.
  • Podcast «Sobes» (Interview)
  • Podcast «Dva Stula» (Two Chairs)

Computer Science Fundamentals

  • Free Python courses «Python Generation». A series of free Python courses for absolute beginners by professional developer and educator Timur Guev. Timur comes from a generation of mathematicians who scored 100 on the national math exam and a generation of engineers who went on to work at FAANG companies. You won’t find better beginner courses than this series.
  • Free SQL practice platform sql-ex.ru. One of the best — if not the best — SQL practice platforms, and it’s free. It features a huge number of exercises. I recommend working through them to solidify your SQL query-writing skills. Don’t let the outdated interface put you off.
  • «System Design Interview,» Alex Xu

Data Science Fundamentals

  • Article «Machine Learning for People,» vas3k. A comprehensive introduction for anyone who finally wants to make sense of machine learning — in plain language, without formulas or theorems, with real-world problem examples and their solutions.
  • «Machine Learning for Humans,» Vishal Maini, Samir Sabri

Inspiring Stories

  • «Elon Musk: Tesla, SpaceX, and the Quest for a Fantastic Future,» Ashlee Vance. The story of Musk’s development as a businessman — the obstacles he overcame, the risks he took. Including a trip to Russia in 2001 to try to buy an intercontinental ballistic missile.
  • «Pour Your Heart Into It: How Starbucks Built a Company One Cup at a Time,» Dori Jones Yang, Howard Schultz
  • «The Yandex Book,» Dmitry Sokolov-Mitrich. The story of Yandex’s rise — from its origins to its IPO. About the personalities of its founders. About how Sergey Brin and Larry Page came to Moscow in 2003 to acquire the company, but Arkady Volozh and Ilya Segalovich turned them down — and went on to build Russia’s most innovative tech company.

item.title: Tools and Services for Product Managers
item.description:
I want to share the services and tools I regularly use to get work done. Maybe you’ll discover something new and make your workday a little more comfortable.

Product Awareness and UX

  • ProductHunt — the go-to resource for developing a broad product sense. It helps you stay on top of new product launches and the evolution of existing ones.
  • UserOnboard — a library of detailed UX teardowns of popular services like Gmail, Instagram, Apple Music, Netflix, and more.

Research and A/B Testing

  • Statista — a knowledge base with up-to-date market analytics and research. A corporate account with access to detailed reports is great, but the free version still lets you browse basic reports.
  • Yandex Wordstat — useful for analyzing user search queries in the Russian-language internet segment.
  • ResearchGate — a vast library of academic papers on virtually any topic.
  • Evan’s Awesome A/B Tools — one of the oldest and most popular online tools for planning and analyzing A/B tests: sample size estimation and experiment result evaluation.
  • GoodUI — a pattern library featuring A/B tests and breakdowns of their results.

Diagrams, Flowcharts, and Graphics

  • Miro — the de facto standard for visual collaboration.
  • Mermaid — a tool for generating diagrams from text descriptions (code). Integrates with many modern wiki systems: Notion, Google Docs, Confluence.
  • Draw.io — a simple and convenient tool for creating more complex diagrams and flowcharts than Mermaid supports. Lets you save source files to Google Drive and requires no registration or login.
  • Canva — the best tool for creating graphic assets. The free version is more than enough for most everyday tasks.
  • Emojipedia — an emoji reference for adding a touch of personality to requirements docs and task descriptions.

Personal and Team Productivity

  • Things — a clean and beautifully designed to-do app for Mac and iOS, perfect for design perfectionists who appreciate minimalism and good typography.
  • Ilya Birman’s Typography Layout — a keyboard layout for writing polished text and typing the right symbols quickly (✓≈≠₽x↓−""). If you write a lot and care about how your text looks, give Birman’s layout a try — it’s a joy to use.
  • Obsidian — an app for organizing notes in Markdown (.md) format.
  • ChatGPT — a replacement for Google search.
  • Google Sheets, Slides, Colab — the bare essentials for any product manager.

Rapid MVP Development and Vibe Coding

  • Cursor IDE — a code editor on steroids that lets you build apps and services with minimal programming knowledge, and do it fast.
  • GitHub / GitHub Pages — deploy static sites to production quickly and for free.
  • Vercel — deploy more complex services to production quickly and for free.
